opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think safety-case regulation is one of the most underrated ideas in this whole debate, because it flips the burden of proof to where it belongs.

Right now, AI is the only industry I can think of where you can build something potentially very dangerous and just release it, and the public has to prove it's harmful afterward. That's not how we do it with drugs, airplanes, or nuclear reactors. If you want to sell a new medicine, you don't get to say "trust us." You go to the FDA with a safety case: here's the evidence, here are the clinical trials, here's why the benefits outweigh the risks. The burden is on you.

If we did that with AI, I think it would change companies' technical decisions in very healthy ways. Today the incentive is to scale as fast as possible and maybe bolt some safety on afterward, red-teaming, RLHF, whatever, which is basically trying to train a black box to behave and hoping it generalizes. But if you have to actually *demonstrate* to a regulator that your system won't do certain catastrophic things, like help make bioweapons, self-exfiltrate, or escape human control, then "we tested it a bunch and it seemed fine" won't cut it for the most powerful systems. You'll want guarantees.

That pushes companies toward architectures you can actually reason about. More investment in mechanistic interpretability, so you understand what's going on inside. More formal verification and provably safe approaches, where you can make quantitative claims instead of vibes. More tool AI, narrow systems that are enormously useful for curing diseases or advancing science, rather than racing to build general agents whose behavior nobody can predict.

And the beautiful thing is that the regulator doesn't need to pick the technology. It just sets the bar: show us it's safe. Then the companies, with all their brilliant engineers, compete to clear it. That's exactly what happened in other industries. Safety standards didn't kill the auto industry; they spawned seatbelts, airbags, crumple zones, and cars today are far safer *and* better.

The one thing I'd stress is that this has to apply to the frontier, the systems that could cause catastrophic harm, not some startup building a customer-service chatbot. Light touch for the vast majority, real scrutiny for the handful of companies building things that could genuinely get out of control. If someone can't make a convincing safety case for a superintelligent system, then the answer is simple: you don't get to deploy it yet. And honestly, I think that's a pretty reasonable thing to ask.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the regulator should set the safety bar without choosing the technology, leaving companies to decide how to meet it.

r002.rationale: The candidate explains that requiring evidence of safety would push companies toward more reasoned, verifiable architectures and make them compete to clear the bar.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that safety-case regulation should shape technical decisions in exactly the same way it already does in every other high-stakes industry, and we should stop pretending AI is some magical exception.

Look at how it works for drugs. If you want to sell a new medication in the United States, you don't get to say "trust me, our internal team thinks it's fine." You go to the FDA, you present evidence, and the burden of proof is on you, the company, to make the case that the benefits outweigh the risks. Same with airplanes, same with nuclear reactors, same with bridges. The engineer doesn't get to build the bridge first and then argue about whether it will fall down. You make the safety case before the thing is deployed.

And what that does to technical decisions is profound, because it changes what you optimize for. Right now, the incentive structure in AI is: race to build the most powerful system as fast as possible, ship it, and deal with problems later. If instead you know that you cannot deploy until you can convincingly demonstrate to a regulator that the system won't, say, help someone build a bioweapon, or that it can't be jailbroken into doing things it was explicitly trained not to do, then suddenly you have a very strong incentive to build systems you can actually understand. You start investing in interpretability. You start preferring architectures that are more predictable over ones that are slightly more capable but totally opaque. You start building in the controls from the beginning rather than bolting them on afterward.

I think that's actually the single most important shift. Today, a lot of what passes for AI safety is what I'd call "safety washing," where you run some evals after the fact and write a nice document. A real safety case is quantitative. It says: here is the harm we're worried about, here is the probability we estimate, here is the evidence for that estimate, and here is why the residual risk is acceptable. If you can't produce that, you don't deploy. Full stop.

And I want to be clear that I'm not anti-technology here. I'm incredibly optimistic about what AI can do for medicine, for science, for lifting people out of poverty. Safety standards don't kill innovation. We have more and better drugs than we did before the FDA, and far fewer thalidomide disasters. What safety standards do is redirect the innovation toward things that are actually good for humanity, rather than just toward whatever's most impressive at a demo.

The companies will complain, of course, because right now they're getting a free pass that no other industry gets. But I think the better ones secretly want this, because it would stop the race to the bottom. Nobody wants to be the one who slows down for safety while their competitor barrels ahead. Regulation levels the playing field. It turns safety from a competitive disadvantage into just the cost of doing business, which is exactly what it should be.

r001.rationale: The response discusses safety evidence and gives examples of technical choices, but does not say regulation should set high-level requirements while leaving implementation choices to companies.

r002.rationale: It explains that requiring a convincing safety demonstration would encourage companies to invest in interpretability, choose more predictable architectures, and build controls into systems.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to put the burden of proof on the companies. If you want to release a very powerful AI system, you should have to make a convincing safety case before you deploy it. We don’t let a pharmaceutical company sell a new drug just because they say, “We haven’t noticed anything bad yet.”

And that changes the technical incentives. Right now, if you’re choosing between an architecture that’s a little more capable and one that’s much easier to understand and control, the competitive pressure pushes you toward capability. If you know you’re going to have to demonstrate safety, suddenly interpretability, controllability, and verification become commercially valuable. You might choose a different architecture. You might restrict what the system can do. You might decide you don’t actually need an autonomous agent to deliver the benefit your customers want.

So I wouldn’t want regulators prescribing every technical detail. Set the requirement that companies demonstrate that the risks are acceptably low, have that case independently scrutinized, and let engineers innovate on how to meet it. And if you can’t make the safety case, the answer has to be that you don’t deploy yet. Otherwise, it’s just paperwork.

r001.rationale: The candidate says regulators should require companies to demonstrate acceptably low risk without prescribing every technical detail, leaving engineers to decide how to meet the requirement.

r002.rationale: The candidate explains that a safety demonstration requirement makes interpretability, controllability, and verification commercially valuable, changing companies’ technical incentives and choices.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to put the burden of proof on the companies. If you want to build and deploy a very powerful AI system, you should have to make a credible safety case before you deploy it, rather than asking society to prove afterward that it was dangerous.

That changes the technical incentives. Today, there’s enormous pressure to make systems more capable, even when we don’t understand how to control them. If you know you’ll have to demonstrate safety, you have a reason to choose architectures and training methods that make that demonstration possible. You invest in understanding the system, in limiting what it can do, and in making sure your safeguards actually work.

And the regulation shouldn’t prescribe every technical detail. It should set the standard of evidence, with independent scrutiny, and let companies innovate in how they meet it. But if they can’t make the safety case, then the answer has to be: don’t deploy that system yet. Otherwise, the requirement doesn’t really mean anything.

r001.rationale: The response says regulation should set an evidence standard without prescribing technical details, leaving companies to innovate in how they meet it.

r002.rationale: It explains that having to demonstrate safety gives companies an incentive to choose architectures and training methods that support safety, and to invest in understanding and safeguards.
